summary: This note describes the nose across vertebrates, covering its role in conditioning inhaled air through filtration, warming and humidification, and its function in smell. It compares nasal structure among amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals and fish, noting how the nasal cavity, vomeronasal organ and olfactory tissue changed over evolution. It also covers specialized noses such as the wet dog nose used for direction sensing, the reduced cetacean blowhole, and the elephant trunk.
one_line: Overview of the vertebrate nose, covering its role in breathing, air conditioning, smell, and how its structure varies across animal groups.
key_facts: A nose is a protuberance in vertebrates that houses the nostrils, or nares, which receive and expel air for respiration alongside the mouth.
In humans, the nose is located centrally on the face and serves as an alternative respiratory passage especially during suckling for infants.
The protruding nose that is completely separate from the mouth part is a characteristic found only in therian mammals.
Hair inside nostrils filters incoming air as a first line of defense against dust particles, smoke, and airborne illness.
The wet nose of dogs is useful for the perception of direction, because sensitive cold receptors in the skin detect the place where the nose is cooled the most.
In crocodilians, the nasal chamber is exceptionally long, helping the animal to breathe while partially submerged.
The reptilian nasal chamber is divided into three parts: an anterior vestibule, the main olfactory chamber, and a posterior nasopharynx.
Birds have a small olfactory chamber, although it contains three turbinates, reflecting their generally poor sense of smell.
In many birds, including doves and fowls, the nostrils are covered by a horny protective shield.
In mammals, the nasal cavities are fused into one and typically occupy up to half the length of the skull.
In primates, bats, and cetaceans, the nose has been secondarily reduced, so these animals have a relatively poor sense of smell.

In cetaceans, the nose has been reduced to one or two blowholes, which are nostrils that migrated to the top of the head, giving a more streamlined body and the ability to breathe while mostly submerged.
The elephant's nose has elaborated into a long, muscular, manipulative organ called the trunk.
The vomeronasal organ is lost in bats and in many primates, including humans.
In fish, the nose has no connection with the mouth and no role in respiration, and generally consists of a pair of small pouches lined by olfactory epithelium.

entities.role: openings that receive and expel air for respiration

entities.name: Vomeronasal organ
entities.role: organ lined by olfactory epithelium found in amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and absent in many primates and bats

entities.role: reptilian-like ancestors from which the unique mammalian nose is theorized to have evolved

entities.name: Elephants
entities.role: mammals whose nose has elaborated into a trunk

entities.name: Cetaceans
entities.role: marine mammals whose nose has been reduced to blowholes
